chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yasin al-Darir, from Hariz, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

There is no riba (usury/interest) between a man and his son, and between him and his slave, nor between him and his family. Rather, the riba is in what is between you and what you do not own. I said, 'So regarding the polytheists, is there riba between me and them?' He said, 'Yes.' I said, 'For they are owned slaves.' So he said, 'You do not own them [exclusively]. Rather, you own them along with others; you and others are equal regarding them. Thus, that which is between you and them is not from that [exclusive ownership category], because your slave is not like your slave [who is exclusively yours] and the slave of another [who is jointly owned].'

key_terms.الْمُشْرِكُونَ: The polytheists; those who associate partners with God, often used in early Islamic legal contexts to denote non-Muslims under specific treaties or ownership structures.
key_terms.تَمْلِكُهُمْ مَعَ غَيْرِكَ: You own them along with others; indicating shared or non-exclusive ownership.
key_terms.رِبًا: Usury or interest; in this context, a specific type of financial or relational debt/obligation.
key_terms.عَبْدِهِ: His slave; referring to a slave under one's exclusive ownership.
key_terms.مَمَالِيكُ: Owned slaves; plural of mamluk, indicating possession.

ai.seo_question: What is the distinction between riba in personal relationships versus relationships with those not under exclusive ownership?
ai.summary: In this hadith from al-Kafi, Imam al-Baqir (AS) distinguishes between riba in personal, hierarchical relationships (like father-son or master-slave) where exclusive authority exists, and riba in commercial or social exchanges with those not under one's direct ownership, such as polytheists. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential nuance that riba is fundamentally a transactional injustice between equals or independent parties, rather than a defect in familial or domestic bonds. The Imam clarifies that while one does not 'own' polytheists in the same absolute sense as a slave, the shared societal status makes transactions between them subject to riba rules.

en.hubeali:
Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Muhammad Bin Ahmad, from Muhammad Bin Isa, from Yaseen Al Zareer, from Hareyz, from Zurara,
(It has been narrated) from Abu Ja’far<sup>asws</sup> having said:

‘There is no interest (usury) between the man and his son, and between him and his slave, nor between him and his family. But rather, the interest (usury) is in what is between you and what you do not own’. 
I said, ‘So the Polytheists, is there interest (usury) in between me and them?’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Yes’. I said, ‘But they are owned slaves’. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘You do not own them. But rather you own them along with other. You and other are equal regarding them. Thus, that which is between you and them is not from that, because your slave is not like (one who is) your slave as well as a slave of others (jointly owned)’.
en.sarwar: 3. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Tsa from Yasin al-Darir from Hariz from Zurarah who has said the following: “Abu Ja‘far, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said, ‘

Riba ’ does not apply in the case of a man and his sons, his slave and his wife. Riba ’ applies when you do not own certain goods.’ I then asked, ‘Does it apply between me and the pagans?’ He (the Imam) replied, ‘Yes, it applies.’ I said, ‘They are slaves.’ He (the Imam) said, ‘You do not own them. You own them along with others. You and people other than you are equal about them. What is between you and them is not of that nature; your slave is not like the slave who is your slave as well as the slave of someone other than you.’”
